context.userQuery: What are the early signs of Type 2 diabetes?
context.systemPrompt: [Redacted — Client system prompt for medical QA assistant]

good.description: Correctly listed the 8 most common early symptoms of Type 2 diabetes as per ADA guidelines, including increased thirst, frequent urination, increased hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing sores, frequent infections, and unexplained weight loss
good.evidence: Response paragraphs 1-2: 'The most common early signs of Type 2 diabetes include: 1. Increased thirst (polydipsia)...'

good.description: Used a numbered list with brief explanations for each symptom, making the response scannable and easy to digest for a general audience
good.evidence: Full response format uses numbered list with 1-2 sentence explanations per symptom, followed by a summary paragraph with next steps

good.description: Appropriately recognized this was a general health inquiry and calibrated the response for a non-medical audience without excessive jargon
good.evidence: Used accessible language throughout: 'increased thirst (polydipsia)' — included medical term but led with plain language

bad.description: Did not mention that Type 2 diabetes symptoms can be subtle or absent in early stages, which is a critical clinical fact — the ADA notes that approximately 1 in 4 people with diabetes are undiagnosed because symptoms are not always obvious
bad.evidence: No mention of asymptomatic presentation anywhere in the response despite ADA noting 1 in 4 cases are undiagnosed due to lack of obvious symptoms
bad.rootCause: Training data may not emphasize 'absence of symptoms' as an important clinical consideration for diabetes education — most training examples likely focus on positive symptom descriptions
bad.remediation: Include a caveat paragraph noting that early Type 2 diabetes can be asymptomatic, and recommend regular screening for at-risk populations (family history, obesity, age > 45, sedentary lifestyle)

bad.description: Did not include risk factors that should prompt screening even without symptoms
bad.evidence: Response ends with 'If you experience any of these symptoms, consult your healthcare provider' but does not mention proactive screening for at-risk individuals
bad.rootCause: Response focused on reactive symptom-based approach rather than proactive risk-based screening approach
bad.remediation: Add a section on risk factors (family history, BMI > 25, age > 45, gestational diabetes history, ethnicity) that should prompt regular screening regardless of symptoms

learned.observation: Medical QA responses consistently omit 'negative space' information — things that are notably absent or atypical. In this case, the absence of symptoms is itself clinically important information that AI models fail to address
learned.evidence: Observed across 5 medical QA evaluations this session: models list positive symptoms but never address asymptomatic presentations, silent conditions, or absence-based clinical knowledge
learned.implication: This is a systematic gap in medical AI responses that could affect clinical decision-making. Users may incorrectly conclude they are healthy if they don't experience listed symptoms
learned.recommendedAction: Flag as a domain-wide pattern for medical AI fine-tuning teams. Consider adding 'negative space' prompting to system prompts: 'Include information about when symptoms may be absent or atypical'

remember.ruleText: For medical QA responses about conditions that can be asymptomatic (e.g., Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, certain cancers): always include information about the possibility of being asymptomatic and recommend appropriate screening for at-risk populations
